 Jamal Murray, Nikola Jokic’s unique spot in hoop history | NBA Insider
 By Vinny Benedetto 
 Published November 18, 2026 8:45am 
 + 
 Add Denver Gazette on Google
 Denver Nuggets guard Jamal Murray (27) and center Nikola Jokic (15) talk during the second half of Game 4 of a first-round NBA basketball playoff series against the Minnesota Timberwolves, Saturday, April 25, 2026, in Minneapolis. (AP Photo/Abbie Parr) 
 ADVERTISEMENT ADVERTISEMENT 
 Denver Gazette beat writer Vinny Benedetto takes you around the NBA and inside the Nuggets locker room: 
 NBA Insider
 The NBA has never seen a duo like Jamal Murray and Nikola Jokic .

 Denver’s stars during Saturday’s win over the Pelicans in New Orleans became the first tandem in league history to assist each other 1,000 times. That stat even caught Nuggets coach David Adelman off guard.
 “I had to get that stat read to me multiple times,” Adelman said before Monday’s loss to the Suns.
 ADVERTISEMENT ADVERTISEMENT 
 Initially, the Nuggets’ coach thought about how many times John Stockton must have set up Karl Malone during their time together in Utah.
 “Then, it hit me that it’s both. That’s insane,” Adelman said. “That should be celebrated more in our game. I actually think it’s surprising it wasn’t more of a thing, because that’s a mind-blowing stat.”
 Roughly one out of every six of Jokic’s 6,187 career assists has been finished by Murray. Adelman has often extolled the things Murray does when the ball isn’t in his hands, namely cutting and screening.
 “We use him in so many ways, especially as a screener, because he’s such a good screener,” Jokic said. “He can really set a screen. (We’re) just using his best characteristic to our advantage.”
 ADVERTISEMENT ADVERTISEMENT 
 Nearly a third of Murray’s 3,116 dimes have led to Jokic buckets. There’s sure to be many more in the years to come.
 “It’s not like they’re retiring this year,” Adelman said. “It’s just a testament to both guys and what they do.”
 The duo started setting up each other early in Murray’s rookie season in 2016-17. The first connection came in the fourth quarter of a 115-113 overtime loss to the Trail Blazers on Oct. 29, 2016. Jokic’s elbow jumper off a Murray assist gave the Nuggets a six-point lead.
 A little more than a decade later, the duo has shared a championship, All-Star appearances, All-NBA selections and one unparalleled record to show for their unique on-court bond.
 ADVERTISEMENT ADVERTISEMENT 
 “We’ve played so long together,” Jokic said. “We pass to each other a lot, so it’s a cool achievement.”
 Denver Nuggets guard DeMar DeRozan (10) drives past Phoenix Suns guard Devin Booker (15) during the second half of an NBA basketball game Monday, Nov. 16, 2026, in Denver. (AP Photo/David Zalubowski) 
 What I’m thinking
 DeMar DeRozan is not the first new Nugget to struggle adjusting to Mile High basketball, and the veteran won’t be the last as long as Murray and Jokic are in town.
 The thing that makes Denver’s offense so special is the same thing that makes the adjustment more challenging than it would be elsewhere. Playing with Jokic is unlike playing with any other center in the NBA, and the chemistry between Jokic and Murray can leave the complementary players trying to find a delicate balance between asserting themselves and seamlessly fitting into an offense that’s put up historic numbers.
 Those who pick it up quickly — think Bruce Brown back in 2022 or Tim Hardaway Jr. a season ago — reap the benefits. For others like Cam Johnson and DeRozan, it’s not so simple.
 ADVERTISEMENT ADVERTISEMENT 
 “You just need to know who he is. Special players, you need to learn how to play with them. Some players you need a little bit more time. Some players you need a little less time. You just need to learn how you can give him the advantage, because he doesn’t need a lot. He just needs a little bit of an advantage,” Jokic said of DeRozan, who scored a season-low two points on six shots from the field against Phoenix.
 “We just need to learn how to create those advantages.”
 DeRozan’s situation is a complicated one. He’s splitting his minutes, being an accessory player when he’s on the court with Jokic. When Jokic rests, the offense’s identity shifts significantly and relies on the veteran to produce more. The flip side is defenses are able to focus on the veteran more when Jokic sits.
 The 37-year-old’s skill set didn’t dissolve as soon as he decided to sign with Denver. He averaged 18.4 points while improving his scoring efficiency on a bad Sacramento Kings team last season.
 Through 12 games, consistency has been the issue. He scored 12 or more points in each of his first three games, including a 21-point night against the Warriors. He failed to crack double digits in the next three games but started to look more comfortable during Denver’s recent four-game road trip that started in Mexico City and ended Saturday in New Orleans. His performance Monday slowed the momentum of a player who’s going to become a top-15 scorer in NBA history at some point this season.
 “DeMar, obviously, is more successful in a half-court game. The game, it didn’t get away from him. The game got away from our team in general with the pace. That’s not how he plays, and that’s not how I’ve used him. I’ve used him in set-play situations, isolation situations. Tonight wasn’t his night,” Adelman said.
 “On the trip, he was very efficient, very productive and that will be the expectation going forward.”
 Anyone who thinks there’s an exact science to this should check out Hardaway’s start to his time in Miami.
 Denver Nuggets forward Spencer Jones, left, fights for control of the ball with Phoenix Suns forward Ryan Dunn in the first half of an NBA basketball game Monday, Nov. 16, 2026, in Denver. (AP Photo/David Zalubowski) 
 What they’re saying
 The Denver Gazette caught up with Spencer Jones in the postgame locker room Monday to discuss his return from a hamstring strain. While it initially sounded like he would be ready to start the season, Jones didn’t make his return until the Nov. 7 game against Indiana in Mexico City.
 “It was extra cautious. There were still some symptoms (before) that OKC first game,” Jones said.
 “We did one more extra workout the morning before the game. It was still feeling somewhat symptomatic — nothing concerning — but at the beginning of the season they wanted to figure it out. Obviously, the worst part is that you’ve got to build your conditioning as the season goes. That’s what I’m dealing with now. I’ll get through it.”
 The extra caution allowed Jones to do the things the Nuggets require of him, namely chasing the other team’s top scorer around the court without issue, he said.
 “That was the big issue, I think, why we took longer. It’s not like I can ease myself into a game. As soon as I go in, I’m guarding the best player. It’s going to take 100, 110% effort, so we had to make sure we were ready for that,” Jones said. “I can’t just go out and be 80%. You’re going to give up a few too many points doing that with the guys I’ve got to guard. That was the big emphasis and a big factor why we pulled back.”
 What I’m following
 LeBron James sits third on the NBA’s career assists list after passing Jason Kidd during Saturday’s game. Only John Stockton (15,806) and Chris Paul (12,552) have more than James’s 12,092.
 It’s likely the Hawks will be without CJ McCollum when Atlanta visits Denver next month. The veteran guard is going to be reevaluated in four weeks after straining a calf muscle Sunday.
 Continuing a hot start got a little more challenging for the Grizzlies on Monday. The team announced reserve forward GG Jackson will be sidelined for at least three months due to a broken bone in his foot that will require surgery.
